title: Grade of Detached Houses 2026: Determining Grade III and Grade IV
desc: How to determine a detached house grade under Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD: by height, floors and floor area; villas are at least grade III; what grade is used for.
summary: A guide to determining a detached house's work grade (grade III, grade IV, etc.) under Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD and how the grade affects permits, warranty and maintenance.
body: p

Construction permits, building contracts and warranty rules often refer to the "work grade". From 1 July 2026, work grade is determined under Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD (replacing Circular 06/2021/TT-BXD), guiding Article 6 of the Construction Law 2025.
h2
1. What work grades are there?
p

Work grades used for managing construction activities are: special grade, grade I, grade II, grade III and grade IV, based on scale, importance and technical parameters (Clause 2, Article 6 of the Construction Law 2025). A grade used for design purposes (for example fire resistance) follows separate regulations and standards.
h2
2. Detached houses: grade by structural scale
p

Appendix II of Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD (item 2.1.1 "Houses and house-type structures") states that the grade of a detached house, or a detached house combined with other civil purposes, is determined by structural scale; a villa is not lower than grade III (full text of the appendix). The common criteria are:
ul
Height: ≤ 6 m is grade IV; over 6 m up to 28 m is grade III; over 28 m up to 75 m is grade II.
Number of floors: 1 floor is grade IV; 2–7 floors is grade III; 8–24 floors is grade II.
Total floor area: under 1,000 m² is grade IV; from 1,000 m² to 10,000 m² is grade III.
There are also criteria for the largest structural span (under 15 m is grade IV), underground depth and number of basements.
p
Under Clause 2, Article 2, consider all criteria and take the highest grade as the grade of the work.
h2
3. Examples of self-determination
ul
A 1-floor house, 5 m high, 120 m² of floor area, span under 15 m: every criterion is grade IV → grade IV.
A 4-floor townhouse, 16 m high, 300 m² of floor area: by floors and height it is grade III → grade III.
A 2-floor house with a rooftop stair-head (tum), 9 m high: height above 6 m and 2 floors → grade III.
p

Height is measured from the ground level where the work sits to the highest point, including the stair-head floor and pitched roof; total floor area includes basements, mezzanines, attic floors and the stair-head (note to Table 2, Appendix II). That is why most houses of 2 floors or more are grade III.
h2
4. What is the work grade used for?
p
Under Clause 1, Article 3 of Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD, the work grade is the basis for, among other things:
ul
Determining the authority to issue construction permits and which works are exempt from permits – see Which Detached Houses Are Exempt from a Construction Permit?;
Determining the warranty period and warranty amount;
Determining which works must have a separate maintenance procedure;
Determining experience requirements for designers, supervisors and site commanders; managing construction investment costs.
h2
5. Does repair or extension change the grade?
p

If repair, renovation or extension changes the criteria (for example adding a floor makes the house taller), the grade is re-determined after the renovation; if the criteria do not change, the work grade stays the same (Clause 4, Article 2). Maintenance and repair that do not change the load-bearing structure do not trigger the work grade (Clause 5, Article 3).
note

This article is a summary for reference only and does not replace the legal texts. The full grading tables are in Appendices I and II of Circular 34/2026/TT-BXD; for houses with basements, large spans or combined business use, have a design firm determine the grade precisely.
